summary: Supply the vertical spacing, the free-end length, the total shoelace length and the shoelace length without ends and the Shoelace length calculator solves for horizontal spacing. That makes it useful for a practical question that turns up in daily life. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Shoelace length calculator work?
sections.html:
The Shoelace length calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports horizontal spacing in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the pattern); then you type in the vertical spacing, the free-end length, the total shoelace length and the shoelace length without ends (Hidden variables).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Shoelace length calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Horizontal spacing=(2 × eyelet pairs × the square root of (-4 × (eyelet pairs ^ 2) × (vertical spacing ^ 2) + 8 × eyelet pairs × (vertical spacing ^ 2) + (shoelace length without ends ^ 2) − 3 × (vertical spacing ^ 2)) − shoelace length without ends − 2 × the square root of (-4 × (eyelet pairs ^ 2) × (vertical spacing ^ 2) + 8 × eyelet pairs × (vertical spacing ^ 2) + (shoelace length without ends ^ 2) − 3 × (vertical spacing ^ 2))) ÷ (4 × (eyelet pairs ^ 2) − 8 × eyelet pairs + 3)
Shoelace length without ends=horizontal spacing × eyelet pairs + horizontal spacing × (eyelet pairs, 2) − horizontal spacing + 2 × eyelet pairs × vertical spacing − 2 × vertical spacing
Horizontal spacing=((eyelet pairs − 2) × the square root of (8 × eyelet pairs × (vertical spacing ^ 2) + (shoelace length without ends ^ 2) − 4 × shoelace length without ends × vertical spacing − 8 × (vertical spacing ^ 2)) + (eyelet pairs − 1) × (shoelace length without ends − 2 × vertical spacing)) ÷ (2 × eyelet pairs − 3)
Eyelet pairs=((3 ÷ 2) × horizontal spacing + (1 ÷ 2) × shoelace length without ends + vertical spacing) ÷ (horizontal spacing + vertical spacing)
Sb7=(-1 ÷ 2 × horizontal spacing − Sb4 × vertical spacing − Sb5 × the square root of ((horizontal spacing ^ 2) + 16 × (vertical spacing ^ 2)) − Sb6 × vertical spacing − Sb8 × vertical spacing − Sb9 × the square root of ((horizontal spacing ^ 2) + 64 × (vertical spacing ^ 2)) + (1 ÷ 2) × shoelace length without ends − vertical spacing − the square root of ((horizontal spacing ^ 2) + 4 × (vertical spacing ^ 2))) ÷ the square root of ((horizontal spacing ^ 2) + 36 × (vertical spacing ^ 2))
M6=(-2 × free-end length − M123 × shoelace length without ends − M4 × shoelace length without ends − M5 × shoelace length without ends − M7 × shoelace length without ends + total shoelace length) ÷ shoelace length without ends

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Shoelace length calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the vertical spacing, the free-end length and the total shoelace length — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Shoelace length calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns horizontal spacing, derived from the vertical spacing, the free-end length and the total shoelace length. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Shoelace length calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the vertical spacing, the free-end length, the total shoelace length and the shoelace length without ends, which is 7 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter horizontal spacing in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Horizontal spacing opens in centimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Shoelace length calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
